newsitem.title: BRAZIL: SOCCER-RIO DE JANEIRO CHAMPIONSHIP CHRONOLOGY.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-RIO DE JANEIRO CHAMPIONSHIP CHRONOLOGY.

text.p: Chronology of this year's Rio de Janeiro championship, universially recognised as the most chaotic in the competition's history.

January 12: Only three of the opening six matches take place because Botafogo, Fluminense and Flamengo boycott the competition in a row over the format. The rebel clubs say they are involved in a pre-season tournament and cannot start until after carnival in February.

January 17: Peace declared after Rio federation allows the rebel clubs to re-schedule opening matches. The format is modified and the tournament divided into three stages. In each stage the teams play each other once. The winners of each go into the final stage. The bottom four teams in the first stage will be eliminated as will the bottom two in the second stage.

February 19: The Fluminense-America match is held up for ten minutes by a brawl which begins when America coach Luisinho runs onto the field and punches Fluminense's Paulo Roberto. Other players and officials join in. The game is the first at the stadium after the lifting of a ban imposed because a rival goalkeeper was beaten up by Fluminense fans who invaded the pitch last year.

March 5: Flamengo striker Romario is involved in a scene that resembles a cheap kick-boxing film as he lashes out a rival defender Cafezinho near the end of a 7-0 win over Madureira. Cafezinho is sent off but Romario is not punished. As the game ends, a brawl ensues with Flamengo coach Junior aiming punches at Madureira players.

March 8: The Vasco-Botofogo game kicks off one hour late because the teams are wearing the same colour shorts and both refuse to change. Directors from the two clubs insult and shout at each other on the pitch during a row over the matter.

March 12: Itaperuna coach Paulo Mata runs onto the field during his team's game with Vasco, rips off his shirt and drops his trousers in protest at the refereeing. Mata is livid after Vasco score a late winner while his own team have three players sent off in quick succession.

March 13: Amid general incredulity, the Rio federation takes no action against Romario for the previous week's incident. He is let off for "lack of evidence" even though the fight was seen by millions of television viewers. Cafezinho is banned for four games.
March 21: America threaten to boycott their final first stage game with Botafogo in protest over the refereeing.

March 23: America fulfil their fixture but their 2-1 defeat ends in a brawl. America coach Luisinho is once again involved. Despite serving a 30-day touchline ban for the earlier brawl, he watches the game from the team bench, hiding behind his colleagues.
March 24: It has now emerged that the first stage will have a "final" between the top two teams. The second and third stages will be won automatically by the team finishing top.

March 25: Vasco are seething when Botafogo, already guaranteed a place in the first stage final, announce they will field a reserve team in the following night's game with Flamengo, who only need to draw to finish second, ahead of Vasco.
March 26: Incredibly, Botafogo's reserves beat Flamengo 1-0. They will now play Vasco in the first stage final, despite finishing eight points clear of them.
March 30: Botafogo claim that justice is done as they beat Vasco 1-0 to win the first stage with 12 wins in 12 games.
April 6: In the second stage, Botafogo lose their 100 percent record in a 2-2 draw with Fluminense.

April 13: A massive brawl on the pitch holds up play for 15 minutes in the Madureira-Flamengo game. Riot police are needed to protect match officials from Madureira playres and directors, furious at a late Flamengo equaliser which they claim did not cross the line. Television replays clearly show the goal was legitimate.

April 16: Vasco's own fans chant "it's a fix" and "robbery" after watching their team score in the fourth and sixth minutes of injury time to beat Volta Redonda 2-1. Volta Redonda had two players sent off.

May 4: Botafogo win the second stage after drawing 0-0 with Fluminense in their final game. They will now meet the third stage winners in a final in which the first team to six points takes the title but where Botafogo will have a four-point head start for having won an extra stage. If Botafogo win the third stage as well, they take the title automatically.

May 25: Botafogo suffer their first defeat as they go down 2-0 to Vasco and cannot now win the third stage. Their final opponents will be decided the following weekend when Botafogo play Fluminense and Flamengo face Vasco. Fluminense, Flamengo and Vasco all have chances of winning the stage and two bumper crowds are expected.

May 27: The Rio federation interrupts to competition at the request of Vasco who have two players picked for Brazil's Copa America team. The rest of the games will now be played when the Copa America finishes, in late June or early July, depending on Brazil's progress. The following Sunday's games are called off.
June 30: One day after the Copa America final, the Rio federation announces new the remaining third stage games will be played immediately.

July 1: Flamengo, involved in a tournament in Brasilia, request their two games -- they had one in hand -- be postponed but the Rio federation responds by awarding walkover wins of 1-0 to their respective opponents Americano and Vasco.
July 2: Fluminense, needing to beat Botafogo by four goals to overhaul Vasco on goals scored, win 2-1 and Vasco, helped by their three walkover points, win the third stage.
July 5: Vasco beat Botafogo 1-0 in the first final match. Only 9,000 fans watch.
July 8: Botafogo beat Vasco 1-0 before 16,000 fans to take the title, thanks to their four-point head start.
